title: How the Tool Moves When the Joints Do: The Jacobian of an Arm in Three Dimensions, Checked Against Finite Differences, and Torque From Force

questions.question: What is a column of the Jacobian?
options: The joint's own velocity and acceleration
The tool's position for that joint angle
The tool's linear and angular velocity for a unit rate of that joint
The torque that joint needs for a unit force
questions.explanation: A revolute joint turning at a unit rate turns the tool about its axis and carries it round at the axis crossed with the lever to the tool.

questions.question: Built with the other convention's rule, the Panda's Jacobian was out by:
options: Nothing: the conventions agree for the Jacobian
questions.explanation: The axis of joint i is the z of the frame before its row in one convention and after it in the other. Using the wrong one gave an error of 1.29.

questions.question: A vertical force of 10 N asked of the first joint of the UR5:
options: 0.000 N m: its axis is vertical
10 N m
8.17 N m, the force times the reach
A torque that depends on the pose
questions.explanation: The first joint turns about the vertical, so a vertical force has no lever about it. The second joint carried the load.

questions.question: What does a tool offset change in the Jacobian?
options: Nothing: the Jacobian is for the flange
The angular part; the linear part stays
Both parts, in proportion to the offset
The linear part; the angular part stays
questions.explanation: Every point of a rigid tool turns at the same rate, but a point further out moves faster. A Jacobian for the flange used at the tip is wrong by that lever.

questions.question: Why is the transpose the force gearbox?
options: The joints and the tool do the same work: torque times rate equals wrench times velocity
The transpose is the inverse of the Jacobian
Forces and velocities have the same units
The Jacobian is symmetric
questions.explanation: Power in equals power out. From torque times rate equal to wrench times velocity, with velocity the Jacobian times rate, the torques are the transpose times the wrench.

questions.question: Why keep the finite difference Jacobian as a test?
options: It is more accurate than the exact one
A sign error in the fast one is subtle and nothing else would show it
It is the one the controller uses
It needs no forward kinematics
questions.explanation: It is slow and a little noisy, but it comes straight from the forward kinematics and knows nothing of axes and conventions.
